name: Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella
credit: Garden fresco from the Villa of Livia at Prima Porta, Rome (c. 30–20 BC), used because no portrait of Columella survives · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella was born at Gades (modern Cádiz) in southern Spain, probably in the first years of the Common Era, and wrote in Latin in the reign of Nero and perhaps a little earlier. He is known chiefly from his own writings: he farmed estates in Italy and wrote the twelve books of De re rustica, the most complete surviving Roman handbook of agriculture, together with a treatise on trees; he is thought to have died about 70 AD.

In the tenth book of De re rustica, on gardens, he broke from prose into hexameters, answering a request from his friend Silvinus to take up the part of farming that Virgil had said he would leave to others. The result, the poem usually called De cultu hortorum, is a Georgic of 436 lines in a Virgilian manner, treating the soil, the sowing and tending of garden plants, and the flowers and vegetables of the Roman year.
